content.metareview:_summary,_strengths_and_weakn: The paper presents a novel LDA-based counterfactual contrastive learning model for text classification and counterfactual data augmentation. Although the method is novel and the experimental results are promising, the paper suffers from a lack of clarity in methodology.  There are several key papers that are relevant to the work but not cited and compared The paper also has major presentation issues. Most importantly, the authors did not address the reviewers' comments adequately.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors present a novel and *simple* approach for contrastive learning by leveraging LDA-based data augmentation at document level; and StanfordNLP-based antonym substitution at sentence level for dissimilar sentence pairs. Existing approaches like SimCSE (dropout-only), SSMBA and MASKER (masking-based), DeCLUTR (dissimilar sentences based on origin document), do not rely on systematic substitution at a document level. TextGCN constructs document representation but does not do contrastive learning explicitly. The empirical evaluation shows improvement compared to non-constrastive approaches as well as sentence-level contrastive approaches.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strengths**

- Interesting novel approach which does coherent (LDA-topic based) document level substitution in order to do contrastive learning
- Empirical results show improvement over both non-contrastive approaches as well as contrastive sentence-level (masking/origin_document) based approaches. 


**Weaknesses**

- Writing could be improved. More specifically, I do not understand the emphasis of Causal Graphs (beyond sounding cool) - yes the LDA based substitution is an conterfactual but it is not an interventional study and claiming "In Figure 3, X denotes the topic words of a document, Y denotes the adjective and adverb in texts, M represents the text meaning, and Z is the text category." is a clear over-reach. Concretely, looking at the example in Figure 1 -- substituting "critics"/"comments" for "bids"  and "Manchester United F.C."  for "Revlon" does not alter the meaning of the document or the category from "news" to "sports" -- it takes the article from *semantically coherent* to *incoherent*. 

- Better details on number of conterfactual examples, average number of words substituted per D+/D- pair and how (topic-based/antonym-based), num_topics for LDA, etc.

- I would have liked to see an ablation study which highlights role of LDA-based substitution compared to antonym-based alone.

content.summary_of_the_review: This is a simple and nice paper. I see following limitations which prevent me from giving it a higher review: (1) The use of Causal Graphs should be better justified (2) Better description in empirical evaluation, and (3) influence of LDA-based substitution versus Antonym-based substitution should be evaluated in an ablation study.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors propose a LDA-based counterfactual contrastive learning model for robust text classification and counterfactual data augmentation methods.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
To help readers better understand the motivations of the proposed model, the authors should not only state them by sentences but also with figures. E.g., the authors state that “However, these models may have learned spurious associations between some irrelevant elements and the final label of given texts.” What’re “spurious associations”, “irrelevant elements” and “final label”? This statement could be further illustrated by figure.

The motivations in the paper are not well-illustrated. The authors claim “we think that introducing the causal inference to the training process of PLMs could improve the robustness of PLM derivative models”. Why?

Why do the authors apply the standard LDA but not other topic models to realize the topic word substitution? There are a huge number of models that are extended by the standard LDA model.

Are there other ways to replace “topic” words in documents?

The contributions of the paper are marginal. The main contributions, perhaps, lie in the way the author augment documents by taking into account counter-factualization. Marginal contributions in terms of models, theory etc.

Other concerns:
Writing of the paper needs to be significantly improved.
The first sentence, “Text classification is xxx, deep learning (DL) models xxx” to “Text classification is xxx, and deep learning (DL) models xxx”
“which is quite a supplement”??

Background and related work section can be shrank. 

The pseudo code of LDA algorithm should be removed. The paragraph “LDA for Topic Words Identification” should be deleted, as most machine learning researchers are familiar with LDA.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper discusses counterfactual contrastive learning to train models that are robust to distribution shifts. They look at several news classification and review classification datasets to automatically construct positive (factual) and negative (counterfactual) examples. To construct counterfactual examples for topic classification, the authors utilize an LDA model to identify topic words that predict the current topic (P). They then replace all these words with words of another topic (Q) from a document that the LDA associates with the topic Q. Intuitively, this new document should have a topic label Q and not P, making it a minimally edited counterfactual. For sentiment analysis task, the authors use the StanfordNLP library to replace adjectives and adverbs with their antonyms to construct these counterfactuals. The authors then train their models using a contrastive learning setup. The authors argue that this can be used to improve the classification accuracy of a text classifier. The paper presents an experimental evaluation of the proposed approach on several datasets and shows that it outperforms existing methods.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
## Strengths:
- This paper is really well motivated and situated in literature. 
- The paper is well written and is easy to understand.
- The proposed methodology is interesting and very scalable, countering the issues that arise from human in the loop counterfactual generation.

## Weaknesses:
- Several details are missing in the experiments section. These are crucial details that can make or break these experimental results. Without these details, it is not possible to judge the validity of these results.
  - How were counterfactual topics selected?
  - What implementation of LDA was used? (The results can be dramatically different between Gensim and Mallet)
  - Section 4.1: “All reported results are averaged over 5 trials”. What changes in each trial? Is it the sample of the data you’re training on or is it the seed?
  - Tables 1 and 2: What is the bolding of numbers based on? What are the error terms in each result representing? What is the standard error? Where’s significance testing?
- The use of BERT and RoBERTa for these experiments perplexes me as we have since had far better models and given the small differences in performance on several datasets, it’s possible that these differences become even smaller, perhaps even insignificant (if they aren’t already) with stronger models like DeBERTa.


### Several presentation issues:
  - Introduction: DL-based or PLM-based —> DL-based or _more specifically_ PLM-based.
  - Opening quotations everywhere in the introduction should be `` and not “
  - Page 6, first line: “Our initiative comes from the that it” —> “Our initiative comes from the _fact_ that it”
  - Page 6, Replacement rule: You use the distinction document-level and sentence-level to distinguish topic classification from sentiment. Sentiment analysis can be document-level too. There’s no reason to insert confusing terminology when you could just talk about topic classification and sentiment analysis just as two tasks.
 

### Missing Citations:
Unlike what the conclusion says, this paper is not the first to study robustness to distribution shift without annotation overhead on the human side. There’s a whole field that just deals with training models to be robust under covariate shifts and label shifts by relying on observational data alone. But even if we consider counterfactual invariance, there are several works that do so. Some examples below:
 - Kaiji Lu, Piotr Mardziel, Fangjing Wu, Preetam Aman- charla, and Anupam Datta. 2020. Gender bias in neural natural language processing. In Logic, Language, and Security, pages 189–202. Springer.
 - Tongshuang Wu, Marco Tulio Ribeiro, Jeffrey Heer, and Daniel S. Weld. "Polyjuice: Generating Counterfactuals for Explaining, Evaluating, and Improving Models." In Proceedings of the 59th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics and the 11th International Joint Conference on Natural Language Processing (Volume 1: Long Papers), pp. 6707-6723. 2021.

Subsection 2.3 does not talk about counterfactual invariance for text classification. It seems very relevant for that. Here are three works that look at that:
 - Jacob Eisenstein. "Uninformative Input Features and Counterfactual Invariance: Two Perspectives on Spurious Correlations in Natural Language." arXiv preprint arXiv:2204.04487 (2022).
 - Victor Veitch, Alexander D'Amour, Steve Yadlowsky, and Jacob Eisenstein. "Counterfactual invariance to spurious correlations: Why and how to pass stress tests." arXiv preprint arXiv:2106.00545 (2021).
 - Divyansh Kaushik, Amrith Setlur, Eduard H. Hovy, and Zachary Chase Lipton. "Explaining the Efficacy of Counterfactually Augmented Data." In International Conference on Learning Representations. 2021.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a method for learning robust text classifiers. The authors propose generating counterfactual examples w.r.t topics by learning a topic model and using the learned probabilities to switch topic-related words. They then train a text classifier with a contrastive learning objective using the original and generated augmentations. In their experiments, the authors show that their method outperforms baselines in sentiment classification and natural language inference on in-domain datasets, and is competitive on out-of-domain datasets.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

This paper addresses a very important problem in NLP - improving the robustness of text classifiers to spurious correlation using data augmentations. The intuition behind the method, that data augmentation approaches should be causally motivated, and that manipulating topic-based information for that is spot on. The attempt to generate a training pipeline that tries to remove topic-related information is also interesting.

Weaknesses:

I appreciate the authors' genuine attempt to create a method that removes spurious correlations with no access to interventional data. However, I find the paper in its current form to be highly problematic and outright misleading.

The causal language in the paper is completely off, reducing causality into an augmentation problem (what are causal correlations? Are they correlations between variables that causally affect the label and they label itself?). Introducing augmentations, even if causally motivated, into a dataset does not “introduce causal inference” to the problem. The task is still a prediction problem, and no identification of causal effect is taking place here (also, counterfactuals are not “essentially a data augmentation”!).

The LDA-based method could very easily lead to text that doesn’t make sense, as different topics should also induce a different choice of words that are not topic words. Figures 1+2 capture very easy cases, so it’s not clear how such a process works when the counterfactual topic should induce a different type of a sentence. Also, how would you enforce the fact that the counterfactual text should still remain comprehensible?

The claim in the paper that “Word substitution can provide a solution to counterfactual augmentation” is very strong. How do you evaluate the validity of this statement? Topic words do carry a lot of information, but doing style transfer with them is extremely limited.

I’m not sure about the novelty of this paper. There are many many papers that propose machine-generated augmentations for removing spurious correlations. Particularly, this paper seems oddly similar to C2L paper, including parts of the abstract which are copied. The results are pretty similar and the authors never discuss the difference between that work and their current contributions. Generally, differences in the performance of C2L and this paper often seem to not be statistically significant. 

This is especially visible on out-of-domain data, which is exactly where we should be looking at. A model that is not using spurious correlations should be worse off on the in-domain data but significantly better under distribution shifts. The fact the proposed approach is mostly useful in-domain is unexpected and seems at odds with the theoretical understanding around this topic (see missing references).

Minor issues:

I can’t understand Figure 3. Why do we have two separate causal structures for one data-generating process? How do we imagine text being generated in the world?
Writing Algorithm 1 (LDA) in its entirety is completely redundant. It’s a direct implementation of a widely-known paper that has been used in similar cases in the past (see CausaLM for one example).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Please see complete discussion under weaknesses. 

In brief, the paper uses “causal” language in an unclear and sometimes misleading way. The evaluation is not done in a way that allows for understanding the quality of the method as a “causal” approach. It does present a novel combination of tricks for generating augmented examples, but they are claimed to hold some causal properties without any justification.

Other minor issues:


Typos: 

“that ask something never happened”
“Whereas these methods yield well results”
“automatically counterfactual data augmentation methods”
“sentence embedding with a mask the irrelevant words”

Potentially relevant references for clearing up the causal language:

1. Causal inference in natural language processing: Estimation, prediction, interpretation and beyond
2. Counterfactual invariance to spurious correlations in text classification
3. CausaLM: Causal model explanation through counterfactual language models
4. A unified causal view of domain invariant representation learning
5. DoCoGen: Domain Counterfactual Generation for Low Resource Domain Adaptation

I appreciate the authors' genuine attempt to create a method that removes spurious correlations with no access to interventional data. However, I find the paper in its current form to be highly problematic and outright misleading.
The causal language in the paper is completely off, reducing causality into an augmentation problem. Also, the LDA-based method could very easily lead to text that doesn’t make sense, and the novelty of this paper seems unclear given previous recent papers on the topic.

content.title: Counterfactual Contrastive Learning for Robust Text Classification
content.abstract: Text classification has recently been promoted by large pre-trained language models (PLMs) which aim to identify target classes with knowledge transferred from sets of reading comprehension tasks. However, derivative models of PLMs still suffer from sensitive performance on different datasets, the reasons are multiple such as cross-domain and label imbalance problems, from which most models may learn the spurious correlation between texts and labels. Existing research requires people to manually add counterfactual samples to the dataset or automatically match so-called counterfactual pairs that are already in the dataset for augmentation. In this paper, we propose a novel LDA-based counterfactual contrastive learning framework and three data augmentation methods, to capture the causal information in texts, which can promote the robustness of text classification. To confirm the effectiveness of our proposed model and methods, we design and conduct several couples of experiments. Experimental results demonstrate that our model works well on five popular text classification datasets on distinct tasks, we find that training with proposed data augmentation outperforms other augmentation methods on many superior models by 1\% or above. Plus, robustness tests on different datasets also show a competitive performance, which proves the effectiveness of our model and data.
